figureFiles.caption: Tetris drawn as a system: the player acts, the rules update the game state, and the state comes back to the player as feedback. Notice that the goal and the player’s freedom to stop sit outside the loop; they are what make this machine a game.
Designers build from mechanics toward aesthetics; players meet the game from the other end. The Tetris row shows one scoring rule producing a well-known strategy and the tension that goes with it.
Fullerton’s eight formal elements and five dramatic elements, each filled in for Slay the Spire. Try covering one box and asking what the game would become without it.

lesson.hook: In December 2023, a 13-year-old from Oklahoma named Willis Gibson did something no human player was known to have done in the 34 years since Nintendo released its home console version of *Tetris*: he played until the game itself broke. Partway through level 157, the screen froze. The programmers had never expected anyone to get that far. For decades, top players had treated level 29, where pieces fall almost too fast to steer, as the practical end. Then players invented ways of beating it, including “rolling,” a technique of drumming the back of the controller against a resting thumb to move pieces faster. Not one rule of the game had changed since 1989. The behavior that broke it was hiding in a short list of rules all along, waiting for players to find it. That gap between a few rules and what they produce is the subject of this chapter.
lesson.overview: This first chapter gives you the three ideas the rest of the book is built on. Section 1.1 asks what a game is, comparing the definitions that philosophers and designers actually use. Section 1.2 introduces the MDA framework, which traces how rules (mechanics) produce patterns of play (dynamics) and, through them, player experience (aesthetics). Section 1.3 gives you a parts list, Tracy Fullerton’s formal and dramatic elements, for taking any game apart. You will meet the book’s running examples, *Tetris*, *Super Mario Bros.* and *Slay the Spire*, and at the end you will write the first rules for your own pocket card game, which you will improve in every chapter that follows.
objectives: Compare the definitions of a game offered by Suits, Salen and Zimmerman, Juul and McGonigal, and apply them to borderline cases.
Explain the MDA framework and classify features of a real game as mechanics, dynamics or aesthetics.
Identify the formal and dramatic elements of a game and use them to find what a design is missing.
Write a first rules draft for an original pocket card game, aimed at a named aesthetic.

sections.title: Defining a game
reading: People have argued about what counts as a game for a long time. In *Philosophical Investigations* (1953), Ludwig Wittgenstein used games as his main example of a word whose members share no single feature, only overlapping resemblances, like the faces in a family. The philosopher Bernard Suits, who taught at the University of Waterloo in Canada, took that as a challenge. In *The Grasshopper: Games, Life and Utopia* (1978), a book written as dialogues between Aesop’s grasshopper and his followers, he set out to show that games do share a definition after all [1]. Designers care about this argument for a practical reason. A good definition lists the parts a game cannot do without, and every part on that list is something you can design, tune or break.

Suits’s short version is famous: “playing a game is the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles” [1]. His full version has four parts. There is a **prelusory goal**, a state of affairs you can describe before any game exists, such as a ball resting in a hole. There are **constitutive rules**, which forbid the most efficient ways of reaching that goal. There are lusory means, the ways of acting that the rules still allow. And there is the **lusory attitude**, the player’s acceptance of the rules just because they make the activity possible. Golf is his clearest case. The easiest way to get a ball into a hole is to walk over and drop it in. Golfers instead stand far away and hit it with a club, and they do it on purpose [1].

Game designers have offered definitions built for their own work. Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman, in *Rules of Play* (2003), define a game as “a system in which players engage in an artificial conflict, defined by rules, that results in a quantifiable outcome” [2]. *System* is the word this book leans on hardest: a game is a set of parts whose relationships produce behavior. *Artificial* marks the conflict as set apart from ordinary life, an idea Salen and Zimmerman connect to the historian Johan Huizinga’s image of the **magic circle**, the special space and time inside which a game’s rules hold [2]. Jesper Juul, in *Half-Real* (2005), surveyed earlier definitions and proposed a classic game model with six features: rules, a variable and quantifiable outcome, values attached to the possible outcomes, player effort, a player who cares about the outcome, and real-life consequences that are negotiable [3].

Definitions earn their keep at the edges. Juul places open-ended simulations, in which no outcome counts as winning, among his borderline cases rather than inside or outside the category [3]. Jane McGonigal, in *Reality Is Broken* (2011), drew on Suits to boil the tradition down to four traits she argues all games share: a goal, rules, a feedback system and voluntary participation [4]. Her list is the one this section uses, because each trait points at a designer’s job. The goal aims the player’s attention. The rules make reaching it interesting. The **feedback system** tells players how close they are. Voluntary participation means the player accepts all three, and can walk away at any time.

Run *Tetris* (1984) through those four traits. Its goal is unusual: in its classic endless mode you cannot win, so the real goal is to clear rows and score as much as possible before the stack reaches the top. Its rules are few. In the familiar versions, seven shapes fall into a well ten cells wide and twenty tall, full rows vanish, and the pieces speed up as you clear more rows. Its feedback is constant, from the flash of a cleared row to the score, the level number and the height of the stack itself, which you read at a glance (Figure 1.1). And nobody has to play it. Because players can quit at any moment, a game has to keep earning their attention, which is why feedback, pacing and difficulty each get a chapter later in this book.

keyTerms.def: In Suits’s definition, the state of affairs a game aims at, describable apart from the game, such as a ball in a hole.
Rules that forbid the most efficient means to the goal and so create the game’s obstacles.
A player’s acceptance of a game’s rules just because they make the game possible.
The bounded space and time, set apart from ordinary life, inside which a game’s rules apply.
Everything that tells players where they stand relative to the goal, such as scores, sounds and visible changes in the game.
The condition that players choose to play and can stop; without it, an activity with a goal and rules feels like work.

example.title: Worked example: is *Tetris* a game under three definitions?
steps: Suits: the prelusory goal is a cleared row. The constitutive rules make it hard: you control only the falling piece, pieces arrive one at a time in an order you do not choose, and you cannot place blocks anywhere you like. Players accept these limits because they make the puzzle exist. It passes.

Salen and Zimmerman: the game is a system of pieces, well, score and speed. The conflict is artificial, the player against a rising stack. The outcome is quantifiable as a score and a row count. It passes.

Juul: rules, yes. A variable, quantifiable outcome, yes (scores differ every game). Values on outcomes, yes (higher is better). Effort and attachment, yes. Negotiable consequences, yes: nothing in your life changes when the stack tops out. It passes all six.
McGonigal: goal, rules and feedback are all present, and play is voluntary. It passes, with the twist that the goal is to delay an ending rather than to reach a victory.
Conclusion: *Tetris* is a game under every definition here, even though its classic endless mode cannot be won. The definitions ask for a measurable outcome, not for a winner.
example.takeaway: A game needs an outcome that can be measured and valued, not necessarily a win; a score that players care about is enough.

misconception.myth: If nobody wins or loses, it isn’t really a game.
misconception.fact: None of the definitions in this section require a winner. Salen and Zimmerman ask for a quantifiable outcome and Juul for outcomes with different values, and a score meets both. Endless *Tetris* and many single-player games have no victory at all, only better and worse results.

practice.q: A marathon runner could reach the finish line faster by taking a taxi. In Suits’s terms, what leads the runner to refuse the taxi?
practice.explanation: The lusory attitude is the acceptance of the rules, including the rule against vehicles, because they make the race possible. The prelusory goal is crossing the finish line, which a taxi would achieve. Feedback and quantifiable outcome are parts of other definitions and do not explain the refusal.

practice.q: Some Pokémon players run a “Nuzlocke” challenge: they may catch only the first Pokémon they meet in each area, and they treat any Pokémon that faints as gone for good. Nothing in the game’s code enforces these rules. Use Suits’s definition to explain why this is still a game, and what it shows about where rules live.
practice.answer: The prelusory goal (finishing the game) is unchanged, but the players add constitutive rules that forbid more efficient means, such as catching many Pokémon or reviving fainted ones. They follow these rules only because the rules create a harder, more interesting game, which is the lusory attitude. It shows that rules live in the players’ agreement, not in the code: software can enforce rules, but players can always add their own.
practice.explanation: A strong answer names the unchanged goal, identifies the new rules as constitutive rules that ban efficient means, connects voluntary acceptance to the lusory attitude, and draws the conclusion that rules are an agreement among players.

practice.q: A company requires employees to complete a weekly points-and-badges quiz, and managers review the scores. Which of McGonigal’s four traits is weakest here?
practice.explanation: The quiz has a goal (a high score), rules (the questions and scoring) and feedback (points and badges). What it lacks is free choice to take part, and its consequences are not negotiable, so it feels like an obligation rather than a game.

sections.title: The MDA framework
reading: In 2004, Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek published a short paper, “MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research,” at a workshop of the American Association for Artificial Intelligence. The framework was not new to them. They had developed it and taught it at the Game Design and Tuning Workshop at the Game Developers Conference in San Jose from 2001 to 2004 [1]. MDA splits a game into three layers. **Mechanics** “describes the particular components of the game, at the level of data representation and algorithms.” **Dynamics** are the run-time behavior that appears when the mechanics act on player inputs and on each other over time. **Aesthetics** are the emotional responses the game aims to evoke in the player as they interact with it [1].

The framework’s most useful idea is that designers and players meet the same game from opposite ends (Figure 1.2). A designer works from mechanics outward: you write rules, watch the dynamics they produce, and hope those dynamics create the aesthetics you were aiming for. A player starts at the other end. They feel the tension or the delight first, notice patterns of play second, and may never think about the underlying rules at all [1]. Salen and Zimmerman call game design a **second-order design** problem for the same reason: designers shape play only indirectly, by setting up the rules from which play emerges [2]. You cannot write “the player feels clever” into a rulebook. You can only write rules and then test whether they make players feel clever.

MDA also replaced the vague word *fun* with a vocabulary. The paper lists eight kinds of aesthetic, each with a short gloss: Sensation (game as sense-pleasure), Fantasy (game as make-believe), Narrative (game as drama), Challenge (game as obstacle course), Fellowship (game as social framework), Discovery (game as uncharted territory), Expression (game as self-discovery) and Submission (game as pastime). The authors say plainly that the list is not complete and that most games pursue several aesthetics at once; their profile of the *Final Fantasy* series (from 1987) combines Fantasy, Narrative, Expression, Discovery, Challenge and Submission [1]. Naming the target has practical effects. A team that agrees it is making a Challenge game will cut and keep different features from a team making a Fellowship game, even with the same theme.

Watch the three layers work in *Tetris*. In the 1989 version for the Nintendo Entertainment System, one mechanic is the scoring table. Clearing one row scores 40 points times the level plus one, while clearing four rows at once, a move players call a *tetris*, scores 1,200 times the level plus one. Four single clears are worth 160 points at level 0; one tetris is worth 7.5 times as much. That single mechanic produces a dynamic every skilled player knows. They stack pieces high, keep one column empty, and wait for the long straight piece. The stack climbs while they wait, and the aesthetic that results is Challenge, laced with tension and relief. The rules never tell anyone to build a well and gamble. They just make it the best strategy, and players found it.

Dynamics include what players do with their hands and eyes. In a 1994 study, the cognitive scientists David Kirsh and Paul Maglio found that *Tetris* players often rotate a falling piece more than its final placement requires. The extra turns are not errors. Turning the piece on screen can be quicker than turning it in your head, so players use the game itself as a thinking aid. Kirsh and Maglio called such moves **epistemic actions**: actions taken to gain information or make thinking easier, rather than to move closer to the goal [3]. MDA has limits worth knowing. It says little about fiction and theme, which Juul argues matter alongside rules in video games [4], and its use of *aesthetics* for emotions confuses people who expect the word to mean art style. As a way to trace rules to experience, it is still the standard starting point, and you will use it in every chapter.

keyTerms.def: The rules and components of a game as the designer specifies them, down to data and algorithms.
The behavior of the game in play, produced as the mechanics act on player inputs and on each other over time.
The emotional responses a game evokes in players, such as Challenge, Discovery or Fellowship; not its visual style.
Designing an experience indirectly, by creating the rules from which play emerges rather than the play itself.
An action a player takes to gain information or make thinking easier, rather than to make progress directly.

example.title: Worked example: tracing one mechanic through MDA in *Slay the Spire*
steps: Pick one mechanic. In *Slay the Spire* (2019), you draw five cards at the start of each turn, and after most fights you are offered three new cards. You may add one to your deck or skip all three.

Do the arithmetic. The chance that one particular card is among five cards drawn from a freshly shuffled deck is 5 divided by the deck size: 50 percent in a 10-card deck, 25 percent in a 20-card deck.

Identify the dynamic. Experienced players often skip card rewards and pay at shops to remove weak starting cards, so that their best cards come up more often. Newer players tend to take every card offered and dilute their decks.
Name the aesthetics. Turning down a reward because it does not fit a plan is Challenge and Expression; finding a combination of cards that works together is Discovery.
Check the direction of design. No rule says “keep your deck small.” The designers wrote a draw rule and an optional reward, and the dynamic followed.
example.takeaway: To make players behave a certain way, look for a mechanic that makes the behavior pay, rather than a rule that orders it.

misconception.myth: In MDA, “aesthetics” means the graphics and art style.
misconception.fact: In MDA, aesthetics are the player’s emotional responses, such as Challenge or Fellowship. Art and sound help produce them, especially Sensation, but a game made of plain colored blocks, like *Tetris*, can be rich in aesthetics.

practice.q: Which of these describes a dynamic, rather than a mechanic or an aesthetic?
choices: Each *Tetris* row is ten cells wide
Players leave one column empty while they wait for the long piece
Players feel their pulse rise as the stack nears the top
The long piece is one of seven shapes
practice.explanation: Leaving a column empty is a pattern of play that emerges when players meet the scoring rules. Row width and the set of shapes are mechanics written by the designer; the rising pulse is an aesthetic response.

practice.q: A designer wants players of her party game to feel Fellowship. According to MDA, which layer can she change directly?
practice.explanation: Designers touch only the mechanics. Dynamics and aesthetics follow from how players meet those mechanics, which is why the designer must playtest to find out whether Fellowship actually appears.

practice.q: Break down the children’s game musical chairs into mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics. Then propose one change to a mechanic and predict how it would change the dynamics.
practice.answer: Mechanics: one fewer chair than players; music plays and stops at a moment chosen by someone outside the game; when it stops, everyone must sit; the player left standing is out; one chair is removed each round. Dynamics: players slow down near empty chairs and hurry past gaps, hover and jostle, and watch the person controlling the music. Aesthetics: Sensation (music and the scramble), Challenge, and Fellowship in the shared laughter. A change: remove a chair only every second round. Prediction: rounds with a spare chair would be calmer, so tension would build and release in a pattern, and the game would last longer.
practice.explanation: A good answer keeps the three layers separate (rules, behavior, feelings), names at least two MDA aesthetics, and makes a prediction that follows from the mechanic change rather than restating it.

sections.title: Formal and dramatic elements
reading: MDA tells you how rules turn into experience, but it does not give you a parts list. For that, many designers use the vocabulary of Tracy Fullerton, who teaches game design at the University of Southern California, set out in *Game Design Workshop*, now in its fifth edition (2024). Fullerton defines a game as “a closed, formal system that engages players in structured conflict and resolves its uncertainty in an unequal outcome” [1]. She divides a game’s structure into eight **formal elements**: players, objectives, procedures, rules, resources, conflict, boundaries and outcome. Her test of the list is to take a familiar card game such as gin rummy and change or remove one element at a time. Remove the objective and play loses its point; change a procedure and the game takes on a different character [1].

Take *Super Mario Bros.* (1985) as a first case. **Players**: one, or two taking turns. **Objectives**: reach the end of each level, usually marked by a flagpole, and, finally, rescue Princess Toadstool (called Peach in Japan, a name later used everywhere) from Bowser. **Procedures** are the actions players take and the methods of play: press A to jump, hold B to run. **Rules** define the game’s objects and what is allowed: stomping a Goomba defeats it, touching one from the side costs Mario his power-up or a life, and a Super Mushroom makes him big. Fullerton separates procedures from rules because they answer different questions. Procedures say what the player does; rules say what those actions mean and what the game forbids [1]. In a paper game the difference is visible on the page, while in a video game the code enforces both.

*Slay the Spire*, a deck-building game from the small studio Mega Crit, shows the other four (Figure 1.3). Its **resources** are many: hit points that carry from fight to fight, three energy per turn to spend on cards, gold for shops, the cards themselves, relics with passive powers, and potions. **Conflict** comes from enemies, and one of the game’s cleverest rules is that each enemy shows its intent for the coming turn, such as an attack of a stated size, so the player’s problem becomes planning rather than guessing. Its **boundaries** are a single run across a branching map. Its **outcome** is unequal in exactly Fullerton’s sense: you defeat the final boss or you die, and a new run begins from scratch [1]. Its Ascension levels, which add handicaps for players who have already won, such as tougher enemies and scarcer resources, raise the difficulty of reaching that outcome while leaving the objective unchanged.

Formal elements describe structure. **Dramatic elements** make players care about it. Fullerton’s core list is challenge, play, premise, character and story [1]. Many students are surprised that the first two have nothing to do with plot. *Tetris* has no characters and no story, and its premise is barely more than falling blocks, yet it grips players through rising challenge and the endless small experiments of play. *Super Mario Bros.* adds a light **premise**, a plumber rescuing a princess, and that thin fiction does real work. Juul argues that a game’s fiction helps players understand its rules [2]. A mushroom that makes Mario grow tells you, without a word of text, that mushrooms are good to collect.

Together, the two lists form a diagnostic checklist. When a prototype feels flat, the cause is often an element nobody specified. A card game with no clear objective drifts. One with no conflict is a puzzle with nothing pushing back. One with no resource that players can run short of seldom forces hard choices. Boundaries need special care in physical games, because they include the shared agreement about when the game is on and off, the magic circle from section 1.1 [3]. You will use this checklist at the end of the chapter to write the first version of your pocket card game. Chapter 2 then looks at what players actually do moment to moment, and Chapter 4 returns to resources as a full economy.

keyTerms.def: The eight structural parts of a game in Fullerton’s scheme: players, objectives, procedures, rules, resources, conflict, boundaries and outcome.
The actions players take and the methods of play, such as drawing a card or pressing a button to jump.
Things of value in a game that players use and can run short of, such as hit points, energy, money or cards.
The physical and conceptual limits that separate a game from everything outside it.
The parts of a game that draw players in emotionally: challenge, play, premise, character and story.
The setup or fiction that frames the action, such as a plumber rescuing a princess.

example.title: Worked example: taking apart the card game War
steps: Players and objectives: two players; the objective is to win every card in the deck.

Procedures: split the deck face down, each player turns over the top card, and the higher card takes both. On a tie, each player puts down one or more cards face down (house rules vary, often one or three) and one face up, and the higher face-up card takes the whole pile.
Rules and resources: card ranks decide each contest; the cards in your pile are your only resource.

Conflict, boundaries and outcome: each flip pits your card against your opponent’s; the game uses one standard deck on a table; it ends when one player holds every card, which can take a very long time.

Diagnosis: every formal element is present, yet at no point does a player choose anything. The shuffle decides the whole outcome. That missing decision is why War is a game for young children and a warning for designers.
example.takeaway: Having all eight formal elements makes something a game, but not a good one; players also need decisions that matter, which is where Chapter 2 begins.

misconception.myth: Dramatic elements just means the story, so abstract games like *Tetris* don’t have any.
misconception.fact: Story is only one of Fullerton’s five dramatic elements. Challenge and play are dramatic elements too, and they carry abstract games such as *Tetris*, which hold players without characters or plot.

practice.q: In *Slay the Spire*, a powerful card costs 2 of your 3 energy for the turn. Which formal element does this cost belong to?
practice.explanation: Energy is a resource: it has value, it is spent, and it runs short. The cost forces a trade-off with other cards in the same turn. Boundaries, outcome and players describe the game’s limits, ending and participants.

practice.q: Which statement correctly separates a procedure from a rule in *Super Mario Bros.*?
choices: Pressing A to jump is a rule; stomping a Goomba to defeat it is a procedure
Both are procedures, because the player does both
Both are rules, because the code enforces both
Pressing A to jump is a procedure; the fact that a stomp defeats a Goomba is a rule
practice.explanation: Procedures are what the player does (press A to jump). Rules define what actions mean and what is allowed (a stomp from above defeats a Goomba). Code enforcing both does not erase the distinction.

practice.q: List the eight formal elements of Connect Four (two players drop discs into a vertical grid of 7 columns and 6 rows, trying to make four in a row). Then name one dramatic element the game relies on and one it lacks.
practice.answer: Players: two, head to head. Objectives: four of your discs in a row, across, down or diagonally. Procedures: take turns dropping one disc into any column that is not full. Rules: discs fall to the lowest empty cell; a full column cannot be used; the first line of four wins. Resources: each player’s 21 discs, and the open cells. Conflict: blocking the opponent’s lines while building your own. Boundaries: the 42-cell grid. Outcome: a win for one player, or a draw if the grid fills. Dramatic: it relies on challenge (reading threats) and lacks story or character.
practice.explanation: A complete answer covers all eight elements without mixing up procedures (dropping a disc) and rules (gravity, full columns, the win condition), and notes that challenge is a dramatic element even without a story.

interactives.title: Landmark games and ideas
interactives.intro: Tap each event. Notice that the ideas in this chapter came from philosophers and historians first, then from working designers, and that the two oldest games came long before the frameworks used to explain them.

events.label: Huizinga, Homo Ludens
events.detail: The Dutch historian Johan Huizinga argues that play is older than culture. His image of the magic circle is later taken up by game designers.

events.label: Wittgenstein on games
events.detail: Philosophical Investigations uses games as the example of a word with no single shared feature.

events.label: Suits, The Grasshopper
events.detail: Bernard Suits defines playing a game as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles.

events.label: Tetris
events.detail: Alexey Pajitnov creates Tetris in Moscow. Its few rules still produce new play decades later.

events.label: Super Mario Bros.
events.detail: Nintendo’s platform game, whose World 1-1 you will study in Chapter 6, teaches its rules through play.

events.label: MDA taught at GDC
events.detail: The framework is developed and taught at the GDC Game Design and Tuning Workshop, which runs from 2001 to 2004.

events.label: Rules of Play
events.detail: Salen and Zimmerman define a game as a system of artificial conflict with a quantifiable outcome.

events.label: MDA paper
events.detail: The framework is published in a short workshop paper and becomes a standard tool of design teaching.

events.label: Slay the Spire
events.detail: Mega Crit’s deck-building game leaves early access; its systems recur in Chapters 3 and 4.

interactives.title: Mechanic, dynamic or aesthetic?
interactives.intro: Sort each statement into the MDA layer it describes. Ask: is it a rule the designer wrote, a pattern that appears in play, or a feeling in the player?

items.text: In Tetris, a completely filled row disappears.
items.why: This is a rule written into the game.

items.text: Skilled Tetris players keep one column empty for the long piece.
items.why: No rule says to do this; it emerges because four-row clears score far more than single rows.

items.text: Your breath catches as the stack nears the top of the well.
items.why: A feeling in the player: Challenge, with tension.

items.text: In Slay the Spire, you draw five cards at the start of each turn.
items.why: A rule set by the designers.

items.text: Experienced Slay the Spire players often skip card rewards to keep their decks small.
items.why: A strategy players discover because a small deck draws its best cards more often.

items.text: The pleasure of finding a card combination nobody told you about.
items.why: This is Discovery, one of MDA’s eight aesthetics.

items.text: In Super Mario Bros., World 1-1 gives you 400 units of time.
items.why: A timer value is a rule the designer sets.

items.text: Players start running and skipping coins when the timer gets low.
items.why: A change in behavior that the timer rule produces during play.

items.text: Friends trading jokes as they pass the controller back and forth.
items.why: Fellowship: the game as social framework.

interactives.title: Why do Slay the Spire’s enemies show their intent?
interactives.intro: In Slay the Spire, an icon above each enemy shows what it will do on its next turn, with the damage number for attacks. Think through each question before revealing the answer.

steps.q: Which formal elements does this one rule change?
steps.a: Mainly conflict, and through it resources. The opponent’s next move becomes public information, so the conflict turns from guessing into planning, and every point of energy can be spent on exactly the right amount of block or attack.

steps.q: What dynamic would you expect it to produce?
steps.a: Players count. They work out each turn whether incoming damage is worth blocking, whether they can kill an enemy before it acts, and which enemy to target first. Turns become small arithmetic puzzles with a best answer to find.

steps.q: Which MDA aesthetics does it serve, and which does it give up?
steps.a: It serves Challenge, because losses feel like your own mistakes rather than bad luck, and it supports Discovery as you learn each enemy’s patterns. It gives up some of the surprise that hidden moves would create.

steps.q: Predict what would happen if intents were hidden.
steps.a: With no information, a cautious player would block every turn to be safe, which would slow fights and weaken attacking strategies. The designers would then have to rebalance cards and enemies. One rule about information reaches through every layer of the game.

slides.notes: This chapter gives you the vocabulary for the whole course. Every later chapter, from core loops to playtesting, uses MDA terms and the formal elements.

slides.title: Why define a game?
bullets: Wittgenstein (1953): games share no single feature
Suits (1978): yes they do
A definition is a list of parts you can design
Edge cases test any definition
slides.notes: We are not trying to win a philosophy debate. Each part of a good definition is a lever a designer can pull, and borderline cases show where the levers are.

slides.title: Suits: unnecessary obstacles
bullets: “The voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles”
Prelusory goal, constitutive rules, lusory means
Lusory attitude: accepting rules because they make play possible
Golf: dropping the ball in the hole is not allowed
slides.notes: Golf is the cleanest example. The goal is easy; the rules make it hard on purpose, and players accept that.

slides.title: Designers’ definitions
bullets: Salen and Zimmerman (2003): a system, artificial conflict, rules, quantifiable outcome
Juul (2005): six features of the classic game model
McGonigal (2011): goal, rules, feedback, voluntary participation
Tetris passes all of them without a way to win
slides.notes: Use Figure 1.1. Tetris has no victory condition, but it has a score that players value, which is all the definitions need.

slides.title: MDA: three layers
bullets: Mechanics: rules, data and algorithms
Dynamics: behavior in play over time
Aesthetics: emotional responses in the player
Taught at GDC 2001 to 2004, published in 2004
slides.notes: Keep the three words separate in your notes. Most confusion in design discussions comes from mixing a rule with the behavior it produces.

slides.title: Two directions of view
bullets: Designers build mechanics first
Players feel aesthetics first
Design is second-order: you shape play only through rules
So you must test to see what the rules produce
slides.notes: Use Figure 1.2. The direction matters: you cannot write a feeling into a rulebook, only rules you hope will produce it.

slides.title: Eight aesthetics
bullets: Sensation, Fantasy, Narrative, Challenge
Fellowship, Discovery, Expression, Submission
Not a complete list; games mix several
Use them instead of the word “fun”
slides.notes: Ask of any game: which two or three of these does it mainly aim at? Your pocket card game will need an answer to that question.

slides.title: Tetris through MDA
bullets: Mechanic: four rows at once score 1,200 against 40 for one
Dynamic: stack high, keep a column open
Aesthetic: Challenge, tension and relief
Players rotate pieces to think (Kirsh and Maglio, 1994)
slides.notes: One scoring rule produces a whole strategy. No rule tells players to build a well; the rules simply make it pay.

slides.title: Formal elements
bullets: Players, objectives, procedures, rules
Resources, conflict, boundaries, outcome
Procedures: what players do; rules: what is allowed
Test: remove one and see what breaks
slides.notes: Use Figure 1.3. Fullerton’s gin rummy exercise is worth trying with any card game you own.

slides.title: Dramatic elements
bullets: Challenge, play, premise, character, story
Abstract games run on challenge and play
Fiction helps players read rules (the Super Mushroom)
Slay the Spire: thin story, strong challenge
slides.notes: Students often think dramatic means story. Tetris proves otherwise.

slides.title: Your pocket card game begins
bullets: Two players, up to 20 cards plus a few tokens
Choose one or two target aesthetics
Write all eight formal elements
Play it twice and record one surprise
slides.notes: Expect version 0.1 to be rough. The point is to have something to change in Chapter 2.

slides.title: Summary
bullets: A game is a system of rules that players choose to enter
Mechanics produce dynamics, which produce aesthetics
Formal elements give structure; dramatic elements give reasons to care
Design is indirect, so test early
slides.notes: Before the quiz, do the practice problems and write one sentence for each of these four points in your own words.

quiz.q: How did Bernard Suits summarize what it means to play a game?
choices: A free activity outside ordinary life
The voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles
A system of artificial conflict with a quantifiable outcome
A goal, rules, a feedback system and voluntary participation
quiz.explanation: That is Suits’s short definition from The Grasshopper. The third choice is Salen and Zimmerman’s, and the fourth is McGonigal’s list of traits.

quiz.q: A player decides to finish *Super Mario Bros.* without collecting a single coin. In Suits’s terms, this self-imposed rule is:
choices: A constitutive rule the player has added
quiz.explanation: The rule forbids an available means (collecting coins) and makes the game harder, which is what constitutive rules do. The prelusory goal, finishing the game, is unchanged.

quiz.q: A drawing app lets players build any city they like, with no score, no goal and no way to do better or worse. Which feature of Juul’s classic game model is most clearly missing?
quiz.explanation: The app has rules (what the tools do), invites effort, and has no real-life stakes. What it lacks is any outcome valued above another, which is why Juul treats open-ended simulations as borderline cases.

quiz.q: According to the MDA framework, which layer does a player usually experience first?
quiz.explanation: Players meet a game through how it feels, then notice patterns of play, and may never see the mechanics. Designers work in the opposite direction.

quiz.q: In NES *Tetris*, one row scores 40 × (level + 1) and four rows at once score 1,200 × (level + 1). At level 9, how does one four-row clear compare with four single-row clears?
quiz.explanation: At level 9 the multiplier is 10: one tetris scores 12,000 and four singles score 4 × 400 = 1,600. The ratio, 7.5, is the same at every level, because both values share the multiplier.

quiz.q: In a cooperative board game, friends talk through every turn together and celebrate as a group. Which MDA aesthetic does this mainly serve?
quiz.explanation: Fellowship is the game as social framework. Narrative is drama, Sensation is sense-pleasure and Submission is the game as pastime.

quiz.q: *Slay the Spire* shows each enemy’s intent for its next turn. Which formal element does this rule shape most directly?
quiz.explanation: Showing intent changes the nature of the conflict, from guessing what the opponent will do to planning against known moves.

quiz.q: A prototype card game has players, an objective and clear rules, but every player can always afford every card, so turns involve no trade-offs. Which formal element is underdesigned?
quiz.explanation: A resource only forces choices if players can run short of it. Premise is a dramatic element, and boundaries and players are not the source of the missing trade-offs.

challenge.title: An MDA breakdown of a game you know well
challenge.prompt: Choose a game you have played for at least ten hours, digital or physical. List five of its mechanics, as precisely as you can (numbers where possible). For each mechanic, describe one dynamic it produces in real play, and name the MDA aesthetic or aesthetics that dynamic supports. Finish by picking the one mechanic you think matters most to the game’s experience, and predict what would happen to the dynamics if it were removed or changed.
challenge.deliverable: A five-row table (mechanic, dynamic, aesthetic) followed by a paragraph of 150 to 250 words on the most important mechanic and your prediction.
rubric: Mechanics are stated as rules or values, not as behaviors or feelings
Each dynamic plausibly follows from its mechanic and describes what players actually do
Aesthetics use MDA’s eight terms accurately
The prediction reasons from mechanic to dynamic to aesthetic rather than simply asserting an outcome

challenge.title: Your pocket card game, version 0.1
challenge.prompt: Start the game you will improve in every chapter of this book. It must be for two players, use no more than 20 cards (index cards cut in half are ideal) plus a few coins or tokens, and play in about ten minutes. First choose one or two MDA aesthetics you want players to feel. Then write one sentence for each of Fullerton’s eight formal elements. Make the cards, play the game twice against yourself, taking both seats, and note one thing that happened which your rules did not plan for.
challenge.deliverable: Your target aesthetics (one sentence on why), a rules sheet of no more than 300 words that covers all eight formal elements, a list of your cards, and three to five sentences of notes from your two solo plays.
rubric: Names one or two target aesthetics using MDA terms and explains the choice
Covers all eight formal elements, with procedures and rules kept distinct
Includes at least one resource players can run short of and at least one real decision on each turn
Playtest notes describe an actual dynamic observed in play, not just intentions

readings.citation: Salen, K., & Zimmerman, E. (2003). Rules of play: Game design fundamentals. MIT Press.
readings.why: The fullest treatment of games as systems. Read the chapters on defining games and on games as systems for sections 1.1 and 1.2.

readings.citation: Hunicke, R., LeBlanc, M., & Zubek, R. (2004). MDA: A formal approach to game design and game research. In Proceedings of the AAAI Workshop on Challenges in Game AI (Technical Report WS-04-04, pp. 1–5). AAAI Press.
readings.why: The original MDA paper is only five pages. Read it in full, including the eight aesthetics and the example game profiles.

readings.citation: Fullerton, T. (2024). Game design workshop: A playcentric approach to creating innovative games (5th ed.). CRC Press.
readings.why: The standard studio-style design textbook. Chapters 3 and 4 cover formal and dramatic elements, with exercises you can do with a deck of cards.

readings.citation: Suits, B. (2014). The grasshopper: Games, life and utopia (3rd ed.). Broadview Press.
readings.why: Short, witty and still the most careful definition of game playing. The current edition includes an introduction by Thomas Hurka.

readings.citation: Juul, J. (2005). Half-real: Video games between real rules and fictional worlds. MIT Press.
readings.why: Chapter 2, “Video Games and the Classic Game Model,” sets out Juul’s six features and their borderline cases.

videos.search: MDA framework mechanics dynamics aesthetics game design lecture
videos.why: Choose a lecture from a university course or a design conference. Check that it uses aesthetics to mean player emotions, as the original paper does.

videos.search: Classic Tetris World Championship final rolling
videos.why: Watch how top players build a well and wait for the long piece, the dynamic described in section 1.2, and how fast the pieces fall at high levels.

videos.search: Slay the Spire enemy intent deck building explained
videos.why: Look for how players read enemy intents and decide whether to block or attack, and for discussion of skipping card rewards.

images.why: The Soviet computer on which the first version of Tetris was written. Notice how little it offers in graphics; the game was built from rules, not visuals.
The seven four-block shapes are the whole cast of Tetris. Count how many distinct ways each one can be rotated, which is part of what players compute on every drop.
The console Super Mario Bros. was first released on in Japan in 1985. Compare its two-button controller with the procedures listed in section 1.3.

review.by: Researched and written with web-search verification; then fact-checked independently by a second agent using web search (WebSearch worked; direct page fetches failed on DNS, so some details such as Fullerton's 5th-edition section headings and the GDC workshop staffing were checked from expert knowledge and softened where uncertain); every answer key re-solved blind.

corrections.before: Its goal is unusual: you cannot win, so the real goal is to clear rows and score as much as possible before the stack reaches the top.
corrections.after: Its goal is unusual: in its classic endless mode you cannot win, so the real goal is to clear rows and score as much as possible before the stack reaches the top.
corrections.why: Not all Tetris modes are unwinnable: NES and Game Boy Tetris (1989) have a B-Type mode that ends in success once 25 lines are cleared, and modern versions have 40-line sprints. The claim holds for the endless (A-Type/marathon) mode the chapter discusses.

corrections.before: Conclusion: *Tetris* is a game under every definition here, even though no one can win it.
corrections.after: Conclusion: *Tetris* is a game under every definition here, even though its classic endless mode cannot be won.
corrections.why: Same issue: NES/Game Boy B-Type mode is won by clearing 25 lines; only the endless mode has no win.

corrections.before: *Tetris* and many single-player games have no victory at all, only better and worse results.
corrections.after: Endless *Tetris* and many single-player games have no victory at all, only better and worse results.
corrections.why: Some Tetris modes (NES/Game Boy B-Type, 40-line sprint) do have a completion condition.

corrections.before: delay the end (no way to win)
corrections.after: delay the end (endless mode: no win)
corrections.why: Only the endless mode has no win; B-Type modes end in success after 25 lines.

corrections.before: Kirsh and Maglio called such moves **epistemic actions**: actions taken to gain information rather than to change the world [3].
corrections.after: Kirsh and Maglio called such moves **epistemic actions**: actions taken to gain information or make thinking easier, rather than to move closer to the goal [3].
corrections.why: Kirsh and Maglio contrast epistemic actions with pragmatic actions, which bring the agent physically closer to a goal. Epistemic actions do change the world (the piece really rotates); what distinguishes them is that they are done to uncover information or simplify mental computation. The chapter's own key-term definition already says this correctly.

corrections.before: **Objectives**: reach the flagpole at the end of each level and, finally, rescue Princess Toadstool (later renamed Peach) from Bowser.
corrections.after: **Objectives**: reach the end of each level, usually marked by a flagpole, and, finally, rescue Princess Toadstool (called Peach in Japan, a name later used everywhere) from Bowser.
corrections.why: Castle levels (World x-4) end at the bridge and axe, not a flagpole. The princess was named Peach in the Japanese original from 1985; Toadstool was the English localization name, replaced by Peach in the West in the 1990s, so 'later renamed' misstates the history.

corrections.before: Its Ascension levels, which add handicaps for players who have already won, raise the difficulty of reaching that outcome without touching the other elements.
corrections.after: Its Ascension levels, which add handicaps for players who have already won, such as tougher enemies and scarcer resources, raise the difficulty of reaching that outcome while leaving the objective unchanged.
corrections.why: Ascension modifiers directly change other formal elements: deadlier normal enemies, elites and bosses (conflict), and lower max HP, starting damaged, fewer potion slots and higher shop prices (resources). They do not leave the other elements untouched.

corrections.before: Fullerton’s list is challenge, play, premise, character and story [1].
corrections.after: Fullerton’s core list is challenge, play, premise, character and story [1].
corrections.why: Her chapter 'Working with Dramatic Elements' also treats world building and the dramatic arc (in the editions this checker knows; the 5th-edition section list could not be confirmed by search). Calling these five 'the list' overstates its closure; 'core list' is safe.

corrections.before: On a tie, each player puts down three cards face down and one face up, and the higher face-up card takes the whole pile.
corrections.after: On a tie, each player puts down one or more cards face down (house rules vary, often one or three) and one face up, and the higher face-up card takes the whole pile.
corrections.why: War has no single authoritative rule here; common published rules use one face-down card, and three is a widespread variant. Stating three as the rule is too specific.

corrections.before: Hunicke, LeBlanc and Zubek begin teaching the framework at the Game Design and Tuning Workshop.
corrections.after: The framework is developed and taught at the GDC Game Design and Tuning Workshop, which runs from 2001 to 2004.
corrections.why: The MDA paper says only that MDA was developed and taught as part of the workshop at GDC San Jose 2001–2004; it does not establish that all three authors began teaching it together in 2001 (Marc LeBlanc led the workshop, whose staff changed over the years). Could not confirm the stronger claim.

corrections.before: and that the games came long before the frameworks used to explain them
corrections.after: and that the two oldest games came long before the frameworks used to explain them
corrections.why: The timeline itself places Slay the Spire (2019) after Rules of Play (2003) and the MDA paper (2004), so not all the games came before the frameworks.

corrections.before: The current edition adds an introduction by Thomas Hurka.
corrections.after: The current edition includes an introduction by Thomas Hurka.
corrections.why: Hurka's introduction first appeared in the 2005 Broadview edition, so it is not new to the 2014 third edition.

review.summary: The chapter is accurate on its load-bearing facts: Willis Gibson's level-157 crash, NES Tetris scoring and the 7.5 ratio, the MDA paper (venue, WS-04-04, pp. 1–5, definitions, eight aesthetics, Final Fantasy profile), Kirsh and Maglio 1994, Suits, Salen and Zimmerman, Juul's six features and borderline cases, McGonigal, Fullerton 5th ed. (2024) and the gin rummy exercise, and Slay the Spire's mechanics all check out, and all 14 answer keys are correct. The one real error is the claim that Ascension leaves the other formal elements untouched; the remaining fixes soften overgeneralizations (Tetris 'cannot be won', epistemic actions 'not changing the world', the Peach naming, flagpoles, War's tie rule, timeline wording).
